item.title: Someone Was Impersonating Her in Online Affairs. She Says It Was Her Husband.
item.description:
As evening approached on a Thursday in late March, Collien Monica Fernandes, a German actress and television personality, was growing restless. She was having an especially hectic day, shooting an episode of a TV series in a busy marketplace in Phu Quoc, Vietnam. The extras needed wrangling; the set was adjusted and readjusted. As the hours wore on, she checked her phone compulsively — she wanted to be alone in her room by 6 p.m. Finally, at 5:45, with the tropical light dimming, the director called it a wrap. Fernandes tore off her costume, raced to her nearby beachside hotel suite and made sure the digital “Do Not Disturb” sign was on. No one who worked on the show had any idea of what she was about to do.

Fernandes had recently finalized her divorce from another celebrity, an actor and comedian named Christian Ulmen. Ulmen was famous for being a master of cringe humor, or as the Germans call it with more precision, fremdscham (“someone else’s embarrassment”) humor — the kind that comes from watching another person experience an excruciatingly humiliating situation. In his most successful show, “Jerks,” Ulmen played a hapless actor and comedian also named Christian, whose desperate efforts to avoid awkward scenarios only dig him into deeper holes of shame. Escorts, sexual insecurities and fecal preoccupations feature prominently in the show, as do elaborate lies that pile up and eventually collapse beneath the men who lean on them.

Over the course of their 14-year marriage, Fernandes and Ulmen were a high-profile couple in Germany and the media covered their relationship regularly, often presenting it as a modern egalitarian marriage that reflected strong feminist values. After they had a child in 2012, Fernandes started speaking in interviews about the double standards applied to working mothers; she published a series of children’s books challenging traditional gender roles and produced a three-part documentary about the history of feminism. Ulmen, meanwhile, made news by declaring that he was taking a year off after their daughter was born.

At times, the public attention felt uncomfortable or outright invasive. When Fernandes gave birth to their daughter, she said, tabloids knew even before she had left the hospital room. Ulmen was obsessive about preserving their privacy — a journalist who was a friend of Ulmen’s wrote in a magazine profile that Ulmen seriously considered moving when the package delivery man started asking too many friendly questions. More troublingly, Fernandes was subjected to disturbing online harassment that went far beyond the usual comments about a female celebrity’s appearance. For years someone, or multiple people, had been impersonating her on social media, starting online affairs with men and creating and sharing or just recirculating pornography purportedly of her — material that featured other women who resembled her or imagery that might have been A.I.-generated. Others were charging money for the promise of access to her.

Fernandes initially did not devote much energy to the problem — how would she ever find these trolls typing away in some remote corner of the globe? — but in 2021, she learned about a video in which she appeared to be having sex with numerous men. She decided to respond as a journalist, by investigating her digital harassers. She was plagued by these shadowy figures for years and after considerable effort, she believed she had finally found one of them, a man who was conducting sexually explicit online affairs in her name. That March evening, she was ready to expose him.

The action Fernandes was about to take would dominate the news in Germany for weeks, inciting a nationwide movement that many would compare to #MeToo in the United States. Alone in her hotel suite, she prepared a post on Instagram to go up around the same time as the publication of a major news report about her experiences. She announced to her quarter of a million followers that she had filed a criminal complaint in Spain, where she had been living for the past few years, against a man she believed was responsible for digital and psychological abuse. “The perpetrator was (as I now know) quite close the whole time,” she wrote. “His name: Christian Ulmen.”

Fernandes first learned in 2020 that she was being impersonated. Men began reaching out to her team, each with a similar, bizarre request: They wanted to confirm that it was, in fact, the real Collien Fernandes who was flirting with them on social media, who sent them nude photos and videos of herself, who was engaging in phone sex with them. Fernandes started to sense the magnitude of the problem when a lunch with a producer took a strange turn — he was clearly under the impression they were in some kind of online affair. “Suddenly he was showing me photos of me in bikinis — erotic photos,” she says. Fernandes made it clear she would never have sent him those kinds of photos and she had no idea who had.

By then, Fernandes had been married for nearly a decade. She and Ulman met in 2010, when he was 34 — already a well-established director and actor — and she was 28, a presenter on a popular music video channel in Germany. That spring, Fernandes had posed seductively on the cover of the men’s fashion magazine FHM Germany, which named her the sexiest woman in the world. Soon afterward, Ulmen cast her as his wife on a show he was making called “The Snobs,” which was set over 18 holes on a golf course, with Ulmen playing an insufferable, self-made businessman.

Fame had made Fernandes skittish about dating, especially as she felt people underestimated her because of her public image. The tabloids often characterized her as a “party girl,” because she was frequently photographed at celebrity events; but Fernandes considered herself something of a nerd. She was driven, even a workaholic, an obsessive researcher with a critical eye. The network she worked for, she recalls, wanted her to be bubbly, ask inane questions and keep things light, which wasn’t really her sensibility: She had an irreverent edge, and would sometimes go off script on live shows, which could get her into trouble with producers, even if the audience seemed to appreciate it.

Fernandes and Ulmen hit it off on the set of “The Snobs.” On their first date, Fernandes recalls, they talked for nine straight hours. They both started out on camera early, as teenagers, and they found in each other something of a haven. “We could have really deep conversations,” Fernandes told me. Neither had much interest in Germany’s celebrity-circuit nightlife; they preferred to stay home, talking late into the night about the people in their lives, their gripes with the industry or what made a scene funny. “It looks like German television now has a new dream couple,” an entertainment magazine wrote after they went public with their relationship.

Fernandes successfully transitioned out of her younger starlet image, becoming a pundit and journalist, while still acting; Ulmen’s work was widely lauded in the press, even if it sometimes courted controversy. He occasionally appeared in sketches, interviewed celebrities or gave interviews in character as his comic alter ego, a boorish, offensive figure named Uwe Wöllner who was prone to crude sexism. As Wöllner, he hosted a hidden-camera show called “Who Wants to [Expletive] My Girlfriend,” in which women in relationships competed to see which of them could most easily lure other men into going on a date or even having sex (promised but never delivered). Ulmen characterized the work as feminist satire that skewered male sexual desperation, but he sometimes joked about identifying with Wöllner’s adolescent impulses. “I, too, have wondered if it isn’t actually the case that I’m really Uwe Wöllner,” he told a magazine in 2013, “and only pretend to be Christian Ulmen the rest of the time.”

Fernandes also sometimes felt confused by the two versions of Ulmen — the one who presented himself to the public as a feminist and the one she says she saw in her own home. After announcing that he was taking a year of parental leave, Ulmen resumed working. In later years, Ulmen sometimes parented solo while she was on location, but she says he was often resentful and jealous. Seemingly small irritations were enough to provoke his anger, such as the placement of a package in the hallway or her mentioning something in the press that he considered private, like the kind of cookie they preferred. (Ulmen’s lawyer did not respond to multiple requests for comment.)

In the criminal complaint she filed in Spain in December 2025, Fernandes portrayed their domestic life as volatile; she said she never knew when Ulmen might lose control. She alleged physical abuse. In 2023, people near their home in Mallorca heard a woman screaming for help from a window and someone called the police. The officers brought both Fernandes and Ulmen to the station, and Ulmen was held overnight on suspicion of domestic violence. No proceedings were pursued by the authorities, and Ulmen’s lawyer has denied that there was any one-sided violence or threats during that incident.

In legal proceedings over press coverage, Ulmen’s lawyer tried to challenge the reporting of physical violence and threats against Fernandes. Ulmen denied Fernandes’s allegations in an affidavit, according to the lawyer. As in all criminal proceedings, the accused is presumed innocent until proved guilty — a principle that has been emphasized in the German media coverage on the case.

At the time, Fernandes told her sister about alleged abuse (which her sister confirms), but she shared none of it with her friends. She had become deeply private, especially after small details of her life were leaked to the media by people she thought she could trust. She also worried that her friends might not understand why she still had hope for the marriage. “I thought I could fix it,” she told me. “I just needed to find the right therapist to help us come out of those negative patterns.” Her husband was imperfect and impulsive, with some serious anger problems, she always thought. But he was also her best friend.

Because Ulmen often seemed suspicious of her interactions with other men, Fernandes hesitated before telling him about her unsettling lunch with the producer who believed they were having an affair. She told me she was surprised that Ulmen asked no follow-up questions — he didn’t even want to see the exchanges — which, in retrospect, she thinks might have been telling.

A chance booking as a commentator on a news talk show ultimately led Fernandes to the active pursuit of her digital abusers. On the set, Fernandes met a lawyer named Josephine Ballon, a founder of HateAid, a nonprofit dedicated to helping victims of online harassment. Their conversation about Ballon’s work hit home: Fernandes was still disturbed whenever she thought about the explicit video that featured someone who looked like her having sex with many men. She decided to make a documentary about sexual digital abuse. The title was “Deepfake Porn,” a topic the project addressed while also exploring other aspects of online sexual exploitation of women.

Fernandes decided to weave her own story into the documentary, even though she sensed her husband disapproved of that approach. She wanted to try to track down some of the people who were impersonating her online; she especially hoped to unveil the person who seemed to be starting digital affairs on her behalf with people in her social circles.

In researching the documentary, she interviewed a man who had been contacted by one of her impersonators on social media. He explained that the fake Collien had initiated phone sex with him on a Google Hangout, but the voice didn’t sound like Fernandes’s. The impostor Collien had also sent him a pornographic story in which a terrified Fernandes is raped by numerous men. It ends with her collapsed on the floor, covered in semen.

Taking in that story and viewing various images of herself as part of her research, she had an overwhelming sensation of shame. She knew these were not pictures of her, or things she had done, and yet they seemed to represent her. They evoked a torturous trick the mind plays when it’s presented with something horrifyingly self-incriminating that is known to be fake but looks deceptively real.

Fernandes resolved to set a trap for the impersonator. She knew that one of her impersonators was operating through a fake Collien Fernandes account on LinkedIn. She and her producer used the producer’s husband’s LinkedIn account to message the impostor account. The plan was to discuss something innocent — an upcoming birthday party for Fernandes — to see if the impersonator would start talking about sex. They anticipated that the conversation might reveal clues about the person’s identity. Fernandes told me she was so enthusiastic and hopeful about the idea that she mentioned it to Ulmen — but the person behind the account never responded.

In the end, the documentary Fernandes made was unable to identify her impersonators, though it detailed some of her efforts to find them. The film aired in December 2024, not long before Ulmen and Fernandes flew from their home in Mallorca back to Germany to celebrate Christmas with their families. They planned to spend Christmas Day with Ulmen’s family, but Ulmen asked if they could stay at the hotel instead. Fernandes described to me what she says happened next in their hotel room: Ulmen had said he had a stomachache; in fact, he had just read a news item about the documentary, which mentioned that Fernandes went to the German police to file a criminal complaint against her anonymous impersonators, something Ulmen was unaware of. Ulmen asked question after question, growing more and more agitated until he was visibly shaking. Finally, he told her to sit down, because he had to tell her something. Secrets he’d been guarding for close to a decade came out, haltingly, she says: He had been impersonating her online.

That night, Fernandes recalls, Ulmen was in a panic. She suspects he feared that the police would arrest him and that he might spend years in prison. According to Fernandes’s criminal complaint in Spain, Ulmen told her that he had messaged hundreds of men over the course of 10 years, but he would not tell her which men, only that she knew some of them. Fernandes, stunned, made recordings of parts of their conversations, which were included in the complaint. She had so many questions: What did he think would happen if he got caught? Why, of all people, had he impersonated her to start a sexual online affair with their pension insurance salesman? Ulmen tried to answer. He was curious to know who liked her. The whole thing felt like something separate from their true relationship, he tried to explain, more like using porn with some elements of reality. (Asked to comment on Fernandes’s allegations through his attorney, Ulmen did not respond.)

For Fernandes, the digital abuse she believes Ulmen committed was more of a betrayal than even his alleged physical attacks. She could explain away spontaneous violence as a result of anger someone struggles to curb in the moment. But she felt this humiliation was premeditated. It was the difference between someone committing murder in a blind rage, Fernandes says, and someone who plans to “murder women and put them in the fridge and give them to the dog.” She believed her husband had not just used her for his and others’ sexual gratification — he had also erased her as a person, replacing her with a depraved adolescent’s version.

Fernandes later obtained and included in her complaint logs of conversations that she alleges came from Ulmen’s laptop that she captured in video footage on her phone. They were, according to the allegations in the complaint, conversations that Ulmen had with ChatGPT over the days that followed, in which the user inquires, for example, about how to ask men to delete emails, without committing some kind of witness tampering.

Fernandes, meanwhile, fell into a paralyzing depression. She couldn’t fathom how she could return to working and socializing with the men in her life, any of whom might think she was crazy, that she had hit on them, that she had sent them pornography — naked photos with her legs spread, violent rape fantasies. She wasn’t entirely ready to end her marriage, much less publicly accuse Ulmen — and yet if she didn’t reveal that she believed her husband was the impersonator, how could she continue promoting a documentary that demanded justice for herself and all other victims of digital abuse?

Fernandes had not made a decision by the time her family flew back to Mallorca after the holiday. In an email that Ulmen sent to his lawyer, which The New York Times has reviewed, he confessed to his lawyer to conducting sexually explicit digital affairs impersonating Fernandes with about 30 men. He also expressed regret. Fernandes told me that Ulmen heard back from a lawyer a few days later, while they were out grocery shopping. She waited by the car in the parking lot while her husband wandered away to hear his lawyer’s counsel.

A lawyer advising a client in that situation would most likely reassure him that in Germany, disputes between couples, short of those involving physical violence, are considered low priority by prosecutors; they often encourage couples to work out their problems in divorce court or civil court (where damages are much lower than would be true for comparable offenses in the United States). An impersonator who posted degrading images publicly would face a stronger legal challenge than one who circulated them to individuals, as Fernandes was alleging; but either way, in Germany, first-time offenders of nonviolent crimes almost never see prison time. In practice, German law focuses on rehabilitation rather than retribution, says James Q. Whitman, a professor of comparative law and foreign law at Yale Law School.

The more Fernandes learned about how little German law was likely to do to deliver some sense of justice, the more outraged she became — not just about her own specific experience, but about the failings of the law to help so many women who had little recourse when strangers sexually violated them online.

Fernandes had been numb since her conversation with Ulmen on Christmas. But when Ulmen returned from talking to his lawyer, she flew into a rage in the parking lot. “So you’re telling me that it’s possible to digitally abuse me and nothing happens — and you think that’s OK?” Fernandes recalls yelling at him. “Do you realize the situation? That you’re talking to the victim?” She says Ulmen told her to get in the car — that she was acting insane. People were going to recognize them. Fernandes was embarrassing him.

Over the next several months, Fernandes wrestled with whether or not she was ready to leave her marriage. “I’m lying in bed,” she told me, recalling the period following his confession. “I can’t work anymore. I feel bad. I don’t have any motivation. I’m suffering.” Her husband, meanwhile, appeared relatively content, she says.

In June, Fernandes told Ulmen to move out. With time, it became clear to her what she wanted to do, which was bring a criminal case against him — but to bring it in Spain, where the couple had lived for the past two years. and where there was a more comprehensive legal infrastructure to address digital harassment, including a court specifically dedicated to addressing violence against women (which many U.S. states have, but which Germany does not).

The news of an explosive criminal complaint was unlikely to stay under wraps for long. After Max Hoppenstedt Heinrichs, a journalist at Der Spiegel, learned of the complaint, he and a fellow investigative reporter, Juliane Löffler, did extensive research and interviewed Fernandes at length. The article they published on March 19 was titled “You Digitally Raped Me” — a quote from a text Fernandes sent Ulmen when she was still trying to convey to him the gravity of what he had done. The article reported that Ulmen allegedly physically abused his wife, impersonated her online and circulated sexual photos of women who could easily be mistaken for her.

The incendiary Instagram message that Fernandes posted from her hotel room in March was timed to the publication of Der Spiegel’s article. In the post, she decided not to mention the physical violence that she says was part of her marriage, focusing instead on the alleged digital abuse. Germany already had laws on the books to prevent domestic battering, but lagged behind many other countries in how it regulated sexual exploitation and violence online. She wanted to focus attention on the lack of those specific protections She hoped that in calling attention to those gaps in legislation, she might help change the law as well as the culture.

Collien Fernandes’s allegations elicited the kind of widespread rage in Germany that was unleashed in the United States when the Harvey Weinstein story broke. Protests erupted across the country, including one in Hamburg with more than 20,000 people. “The shame has to change sides,” some signs said, referencing a phrase popularized by Gisèle Pelicot, the activist whose shocking public testimony against her husband and dozens of men who raped her while she was drugged had stirred a similar awakening in France. Other signs said, “It’s always a man!” and “Everyone knows a victim, no one knows a perpetrator.” A magazine columnist wrote that her inbox was full of messages from women saying, “How are we supposed to live with men?” and that they planned to stay celibate. Leading politicians rallied around the cause of offering women better protection from digital violence.

The response from fellow German celebrities on social media was swift. Benjamin von Stuckrad-Barre, a widely respected journalist and TV personality who had been a friend of Ulmen’s for close to 30 years, wrote on Instagram that his “solidarity and support” belonged solely to Fernandes. An actress named Inez Bjorg David, who appeared on “Jerks,” posted a copy of the email she had just written to her managers. “I would love it if you removed ‘Jerks’ from my résumé,” she wrote. “It makes me want to throw up and I’m so angry.”

The day the news broke, Stephanie Hubig, the German minister of justice, went public with proposed legislation, long in the works, intended to protect the victims of digital abuse. The legislation would criminalize making or distributing A.I.-modified sexually explicit images without consent, an offense subject to two years’ imprisonment. She also called for technology platforms to disclose information about secretive social media accounts so that violators’ identities could quickly be revealed. Even deepfakes or impersonations that were not sexual in nature but caused reputational harm could be subject to prosecution under the legislation.

Fernandes was gratified that those in Parliament were paying attention, but the timing of the announcement about the legislation contributed to a powerful backlash. Commentators sympathetic to the AfD, Germany’s far-right, populist party, along with anti-establishment actors, privacy rights activists and other critics cast Fernandes, in thousands of posts on X, as colluding with Hubig to try to chip away, for example, at the right to be anonymous online.

Other commentators implied, on social media or in the press, that the madness of the crowd was undermining the presumption of innocence, that women were generalizing too broadly about all men as bad actors (“Throw Out Toxic-Femininity” was the headline of one story about Fernandes in a German magazine). Critics accused Fernandes of having posed practically nude anyway, of being a man-hater, an attention seeker, a bad mother.

It’s not uncommon for individuals who step forward with stories of sexual harassment or domestic violence to face a backlash in Germany, says Löffler, one of the reporters for Der Spiegel who broke the Fernandes story and who has published prominent #MeToo journalism. Until recent years, detailed reporting on accusations of domestic abuse or sexual harassment in Germany were rare, and when it did appear, it often provoked critiques from readers and commentators. “You might get feedback like, ‘Why do I need to hear about this private affair?’” she says. Only in recent years, Löffler explains, has there been more recognition that writing about these issues is an important way to expose abuses of power.

It is not only a cultural norm that has often muffled this sort of reporting in Germany. The German Constitution considers inviolate the right to dignity. That principle is understood there to include privacy and the right of “personality,” which is thought to be, at its core, the right to control one’s own image. Although the German Constitution also ensures the right to free speech, courts in Germany are forever balancing the two concerns, which has had a notable effect on the way that the German media operates. In the United States, a public figure who is trying to win damages against a media outlet must prove that it published false information and also showed “actual malice” in doing so. In Germany, public figures can bring charges of “insult” even if the facts reported are accurate, and courts are frequently asked to weigh in on whether a given piece of journalism is sufficiently important to the public interest to justify exposing the personal details it includes.

Certain details — such as those about sexual leanings or revelations unveiled in therapy — may be deemed so private that no measure of public interest would justify their publication. Courts in Germany are also swifter to file injunctions halting publication than their U.S. counterparts. (The right to privacy in Germany extends so far that mug shots and even the last names of those accused of crimes — including sexual harassment and terrorism — are routinely excluded from news reports, unless there’s a strong public interest.)

The emphasis on privacy has often resulted in a somewhat muted media response to cases in which public figures are accused of sexual misconduct. By contrast, in the United States, the initial #MeToo reporting about Weinstein unleashed unfettered coverage in numerous publications about other harassers or abusers in positions of power, as women stepped forward to share their own stories.

Shortly after Der Spiegel published its story, Ulmen’s lawyer quickly announced that he would be taking legal action against the magazine, accusing it of publishing illegal reporting and making false claims, while also warning away other publications from reporting on Fernandes’s allegations. Ulmen’s lawyer would go on to contest the allegations of physical assault, insist that his client never created or disseminated deepfake videos and challenge the inclusion of the email Ulmen sent to his lawyer.

Even though Der Spiegel never stated in the article that Ulmen had created or distributed deepfake videos of Fernandes, an appellate court ruled in June that the article implied that Ulmen had done so because the story explored the phenomenon of deepfakes. The publication was required to add new language to the article that explicitly stated that there was no evidence that Ulmen made or distributed deepfake videos. Der Spiegel was also ordered to delete two sentences deemed highly personal from Ulmen’s correspondence with his lawyer.

Although Der Spiegel had strong evidence to support its reporting, including audio files, documents, text chats and photos, some news outlets were reluctant to reference Der Spiegel’s reporting on Fernandes’s allegations. In Germany, publishers often fear relying on other publications’ reporting unless they, too, have strong evidence in hand. (In the United States, by contrast, once information about public figures is public, other outlets can reference it, unless they know it’s false.) Much of the coverage defaulted to stories about the legal maneuverings on each side.

Ulmen’s lawyer, in winning small victories in court, was able to sow doubt, in some corners, in Fernandes’ credibility or the accuracy of her story. Reporterfabrik, a nonprofit devoted to media literacy, is scheduled to release a report in late September on how the media narrative about Fernandes played out; in an Instagram post announcing the report, the nonprofit wrote that Ulmen’s lawyer has operated by “disputing trivialities and using the tactic of hyperspecific denials — to desperately create the impression that [Ulmen’s] ex-wife accused him unjustly.” They call the approach “a grotesque web of distractions, half-truths and sham battles, intended to disappear behind a smoke screen of flashbangs.”

The right to control one’s image in Germany has also translated into journalistic norms that are not enforced by law but nonetheless give unusual power to sources. People can often expect to have approval over their quotes before they are published. In March, Ulmen spent five hours talking about his marriage to reporters at Die Zeit, a weekly newspaper. In the end, Ulmen opted to rescind the entirety of the interview. “Mr. Ulmen Would Rather Not After All,” the headline of the story said. (Ulmen’s lawyer later said that the interview was always intended to be a “background briefing.)

That Der Spiegel was as challenged as it was in reporting on Ulmen, can seem paradoxical: Out of legal deference for Ulmen’s right to control his image, the publication was limited in what it could say about his alleged digital usurping of his wife’s image.

Although many of Ulmen’s fans defended him on social media, the allegations and the article in Der Spiegel had immediate professional consequences for him. The German streaming service that carried “Jerks” pulled the show from its site. Producers also chose to shelve a new project, a show called “The Au Pair,” that Ulmen had been working on in the months after his split with Fernandes.

Fernandes was surprised, when journalists who had obtained the scripts ran them by her, to see intimate details that she says he had taken from their family’s personal life and woven into the story lines. In one episode, according to journalists who reported on the scripts, a young man admits to his love interest that he has posted pictures of her on sexualized sites, because it aroused him to see other men’s desire for her. The scene ends with him weeping.

“Shame is a pain that hurts less when you share it,” Ulmen once said in an interview, explaining why the men on “Jerks” so often ended up exposing, inadvertently or not, their most base impulses. In another interview, he is described as never feeling more free than when he plays Wöllner, a figure who does not bother laboring under the burden of hiding his shame. In a 2013 article called “My Friend, the Monster,” a journalist friend of Ulmen’s at the time wrote: “There’s one role that really gets to him: being Christian Ulmen. How does that even work? Nobody tells you.”

I spoke to Fernandes several times over the course of the summer. She was still regularly appearing on TV to push for more significant penalties for digital offenses committed against women, while also trying to manage the anguish that the news inevitably created for members of her family. The criminal complaint she filed in Spain with a special court devoted to violence against women was awaiting a ruling on jurisdiction from a higher court; the original complaint she filed in Germany during her research for the documentary in 2024 had been closed, then reopened following the prominence of the news story, then transferred to a different court, and is still in an investigatory phase. A news release from that court reported that prosecutors were still assessing the material they had with regard to both bodily injury and “allegations of ‘digital violence.’”

When we talked, she often looked to be in a state of shock, something that was rarely visible in the dozens of interviews she gave for German media, in which she invariably projected confidence and poise. She often wore a black blazer, an item of clothing she seems to rely on for added authority, even though it’s so oversized that she appears to be retreating into it. Because she’s more petite than people assume, barely 5-foot-4, she used to be able to move freely without being recognized. More recently, she said, she is approached constantly. “I get hugged a lot in elevators,” she said. “The older women — they want to tell me they went through something once, too.”

The last time we met, in June, we sat on her porch in Mallorca. The Mediterranean seemed to hover in the distance, calm and blue. Fernandes told me that she has a hard time relaxing these days; she has struggled with anxiety, panic attacks and insomnia. Ulmen still lived nearby, and she dreaded running into him at the gas station or the mall or even, possibly, at her own front door. She was overwhelmed by the avalanche of attention, some of it negative. At times she even seemed to feel she had to justify why she decided to speak out. She said she had learned nothing from her husband about which men in her social circles had been contacted by her impersonator. “I had to be able to speak up for myself,” she said.

Despite the backlash, much of the legislation the German justice minister has proposed has wide support and could pass next year. Fernandes is now thinking about returning to Germany. Moving to Mallorca had the effect of largely isolating Fernandes, who, even now, speaks only enough Spanish to get by at the grocery store. She has few close friends who live nearby, and the multimillion-dollar homes closest to her are all protected behind high gates.

Her own house feels oddly empty, with two different rough patches on walls where flat-screen televisions used to be before Ulmen took them to his new home. Holes were still visible where there used to be security cameras. Ulmen had arranged for them to be installed soon after they moved in. One of the cameras in Fernandes’s office faced into the room, rather than out toward where intruders might be approaching. Months after Ulmen moved out, the video feed was still available to him, she worried; she didn’t have the passcode to shut it off. Last winter, a friend who was visiting took one look at the cameras and decided they had to go. “Do you have a ladder?” she asked Fernandes.

The cameras came down.

item.title: Man Who Told of a Childhood With Wolves Dies at 80
item.description:
Marcos Rodríguez Pantoja, whose account of growing up in a remote part of Spain, with the companionship of only wolves and other animals, was analyzed in a case study and adapted into literature and film, died this month at 80, according to the authorities in San Cibrao das Viñas, the municipality where he spent his final years.

Mr. Rodríguez’s story came to light in the mid-1970s, about a decade after he had made what he described as an unwilling return to human society. Gabriel Janer Manila, a writer, heard about the case from a friend and wanted to learn more.

“At first, it seemed like a fabrication. It couldn’t be true,” Mr. Janer said in a 2010 interview with the site Anika Entre Libros.

But he came to believe to believe the tale, finding corroboration for Mr. Rodríguez’s claims from witnesses and other research. Mr. Janer would go on to write a study about Mr. Rodríguez’s childhood and, later, a novel called “I Played With Wolves,” originally published in 2009.

The story also inspired a 2010 film directed by Gerardo Oliveras, “Among Wolves,” in which Mr. Rodríguez appeared.

Mr. Rodríguez faced doubts over the years, but his story fascinated many. Mr. Janer became convinced after visiting places Mr. Rodríguez said he had been and meeting people — including a seminarian who had cared for him — who backed up the story and spoke of Mr. Rodríguez’s complete lack of social know-how.

In Rante, a village in San Cibrao das Viñas, in northwest Spain, where Mr. Rodríguez lived for the last quarter-century of his life, some people told Germany’s public broadcaster around the time the film was released that they had doubted his story until it was made into a movie — and some said they continued to be dubious. In 2010, a team from Spain’s public broadcaster traveled with Mr. Rodríguez to the place where he said he had lived, filming him showing some of his survival skills, like catching fish using rocks, and his deep familiarity with nature, including mimicking bird calls.

In any case, he eventually came to be known as the “wolf boy of Sierra Morena” and stuck to the story over the decades.

Claims of having grown up in the wild are widely viewed with skepticism, and expertise in the subject is rare. There have been some notable cases, though they are few. Feral children also appeared in ancient myths and medieval folk tales, fueling a real-life fascination with them.

In 1726, Caroline, the Princess of Wales, sought the guardianship of a youth found in the woods in Germany who became known as Peter the Wild Boy and was a source of wonder in Europe. She installed him in her house in London under the watch of a doctor, then put him in the care of a servant when he proved unruly. The so-called Wild Boy of Aveyron was found in France at the end of the 18th century and was taken to a physician in Paris who tried and failed to teach him society’s ways.

Such tales have intrigued people because they say as much about society as they do about the children said to have lived outside of it. “Through the stories, factual and fictional, of the feral children, there emerges, perhaps, another narrative: the fragmented and haunting story of our continuing relationship with the savage image of ourselves,” the cultural historian Michael Newton wrote in his 2002 book, “Savage Girls and Wild Boys: A History of Feral Children.”

As Mr. Rodríguez told it, he was born into a poor family in southern Spain in June 1946. His mother died when he was very young, and the woman his father later married was an abusive stepmother. The family lived in a remote alpine hut in the Sierra Morena mountain range, turning firewood into charcoal. When he was about 7, he said, he was put in the care of an old goatherd, to be trained to replace him.

“He takes Marcos in and teaches him how to survive, how to care for the flock of goats, how to do everything that might help him,” Mr. Janer said in the 2010 interview.

The old man then died or disappeared, and young Marcos began to fend for himself, unwilling or unable to return to his former home.

Mr. Rodríguez said he lived in the wild for about 11 years with the help of wolves and other animals. In 1965, he was discovered by law enforcement authorities among wolves, wearing animal skins.

He described his return to life among humans as something he did not know how to manage and would never fully embrace. According to Mr. Rodríguez’s interviews and Mr. Janer’s study, his rehabilitation was undertaken by nuns. He said he had lost the habits of walking upright and of using human speech, and he had forgotten how to behave with people.

Mr. Rodríguez said he struggled with human society for much of his life. Employers had taken advantage of him over the years, people had mocked him and he had been happiest among the animals, he said in interviews.

In Rante, he worked with Amigas das Árbores, an environmental group, speaking to children at schools about his youth and his unique experience with animals.

The group, in a post on social media earlier this month, said that one of his final wishes had been “for his ashes to remain in the village that took him in.”

In an interview with the newspaper El País in 2018, Mr. Rodríguez said that despite his disappointment with humanity, he had no chance of returning to a life in the mountains. The area where he had once lived now featured cottages connected to the electric grid, and the wolves were strangers.

“If I call out to them they are going to respond, but they are not going to approach me,” he said. “I smell like people.”

item.title: U.S. Tariffs Could Price Canadian Firms Out of U.S. and Threaten Thousands of Jobs
item.description:
The 50 percent tariffs that President Trump imposed on Canada this weekend could be devastating for many Canadian companies and their employees. It could price them out of the United States and lead to the loss in tens of thousands of jobs, economists say.

“Fifty percent is a huge number for the individual products that are affected,” said Joseph Steinberg, a professor of macroeconomics at the University of Toronto.

“For those products, we should see a very large reduction in exports,” he added. “In some cases, exports will stop altogether, and the firms that produce those products will be severely impacted. Some will undoubtedly shut down.”

Up to 90,000 jobs in Canada could be lost, according to calculations by Trevor Tombe, a trade economist at the University of Calgary in Alberta. Those include jobs at companies not directly affected by tariffs. For example, demand for truck drivers will dry up once Canadian firms are shut out of the U.S. market.

Among the industries likely to be hit hard is forestry. After decades of steep tariffs on softwood lumber — levies that Mr. Trump increased last year — it is facing additional 50 percent tariffs on exports that include plywood, laminated wood products, fiberboard, paper, tissue for toilet paper and packaging.

“We’re getting hammered,” said Derek Nighbor, president of the Forest Products Association of Canada. Nevertheless, he said, he supports the decision of Prime Minister Mark Carney to walk away from trade negotiations with the United States on Friday night.

“This is at a time when the fundamentals of the U.S. economy are not great,” Mr. Nighbor added. “We’re dealing with very, very soft markets that aren’t going to get much better if this kind of tariff behavior keeps up.”

On Tuesday, Mr. Carney is expected to announce retaliation tariffs against the United States, Canadian officials said.

The collapse of trade talks led Mr. Trump to unleash the new tariffs on hundreds of exports from Canada. They cover about $20 billion in trade from Canada. The tariffs arrived on top of levies of 50 percent imposed on Canadian steel and aluminum, as well as 25 percent duties on automobiles that Mr. Trump announced last year.

On Monday, Mr. Trump also threatened to raise auto tariffs to 50 percent on Jan. 1 and to impose the same tariff on auto parts that are currently exempted from payments if they qualify as North American under the trade treaty between the United States, Mexico and Canada.

While $20 billion in trade sounds huge, it is about 5.5 percent of the value of all products Canada sends to the United States. So the new tariffs may not have a sweeping, debilitating effect on Canada’s economy, economists say.

Canada’s exports are dominated by shipments of oil and gas — items that Mr. Trump has excluded from his tariff war, along with the fertilizer potash and most minerals.

For the Canadian economy as a whole, the new levies will increase the effective tariff rate for Canadian products by about 2.5 percentage points, economists say. That will raise the average tariff that the United States puts on Canadian goods to about 6.5 percent, Professor Tombe said by email.

By comparison, Mr. Trump negotiated deals with several other major trading partners that brought in 15 percent in general tariffs.

The Royal Bank of Canada also estimated that tariffs at that average level would affect only about 0.4 percent of Canada’s economic output.

But in an analysis published on Monday, TD Securities, Toronto-Dominion Bank’s investment brokerage, said that the new tariffs were a potential problem even if they were unlikely to put sustained pressure on the Canadian dollar.

“The larger concern is the signal a failed agreement sends about the prospects for a broader trade resolution,” the analysis said. “Markets may interpret this as evidence that trade uncertainty will persist.”

While the tariffs that were imposed on Saturday will hurt the forest industries, they will most severely hit companies that export machinery and electronics, and that produce furniture, toys and products made largely of plastic.

The new tariffs will make it impossible for many Canadian companies to continue to sell to the U.S. market, Professor Steinberg said. About 15 percent of Canada’s economy is directly linked to trade with the United States, he estimated. The U.S. market takes about 70 percent of all Canadian exports.

But the importance of selling to Americans varies wildly among Canadian companies and economic sectors. Upward of 90 percent of vehicles made in Canada, for example, go to American buyers.

Mr. Carney, an economist and a former central banker, has pledged 28 billion Canadian dollars, about $20 billion, to help Canadian companies affected by the new U.S. levies, although details have yet to be released.

On Saturday, he suggested that Canada’s debt would not be caught up in a situation like the current instability in the U.S. bond market.

“We are entering a phase where fiscal strength, discipline, focus, is going to be very important; it’s going to be scrutinized,” he told reporters.

“The way the world works is that markets sometimes ignore these fundamentals. And then all of a sudden they focus on them. And when they focus them, if you don’t have your house in order, it is too late. We have our house in order.”

The prime minister also vowed, after the trade talks fell apart, to match the U.S. tariffs “dollar for dollar” on American goods coming into Canada.

Professor Steinberg said it was impossible to impose retaliatory tariffs that had no consequences, like higher prices, for Canadians.

“Canadian retaliatory tariffs on America, they do hurt America a little bit but also hurt the Canadian economy far more,” he said “Tariffs in either direction have roughly 10 times more impact on Canadian economy. That applies to Trump’s tariffs, that applies our retaliatory measures.”

More broadly, he said, tariffs aren’t obviously effective. The retaliatory levies Canada imposed on American-made autos and other products last year did not stop Mr. Trump from introducing his latest tariffs or overtly damage the overall U.S. economy.

“It’s just going to be a cost for the Canadian economy, but what do we gain from doing that?” Professor Steinberg said. “The case simply has not been made to me.”

On Monday, there were no obvious signs of panic in Canada. The S&P/TSX Index of Canadian stocks closed slightly up from last Friday. The Canadian dollar also closed down by less than 1 cent relative to the U.S. dollar.

item.title: Silence, Wolves and the Wild East: Hiking in Portugal’s Côa Valley
item.description:
The flashlight flicks on and carvings appear out of the darkness. They are 20,000 years old. Engravings of ibex, horses and aurochs, drawn alone or in groups. A few are in movement, like ancient animations. Their crisp lines feel timeless.

I am here to walk as much as I can of Portugal’s Côa Valley Grand Route, staying in bed-and-breakfasts and trying to understand the changes that are drawing both wildlife and people back to one of the country’s most remote corners.

I began a week earlier, driving three hours inland from Porto — past crowds of tour buses and day-trippers in the wine region of Pinhão. Evening fell over the vines, and the lights flicked out one by one until the road wound dark and silent through the hills. I watched a stone marten cross the road, low and dark, satin fur.

My first stop is in the village of Vale da Senhora da Póvoa, where Samuel Ribeiro and Marta Simoes, young transplants from Lisbon, run a grocery store and a small nature guiding company. The couple is part of a small wave of people reversing a 50-year tide that has almost entirely emptied this region, as people fled in search of better economic opportunities. Their store, full of both basics and local artisanal products, is about community as much as commerce.

Marta packs me a picnic — crisp local bread, honey, sweet tomatoes in olive oil, plump cherries — and I set off to find the source of the river.

When I find it, the Côa River wells implausibly out of dry ground among oaks and pines, then runs north along the Spanish border. The area, called the Malcata, is a nature reserve of hills and steep valleys that was the last home to wild Iberian lynx in Portugal before they disappeared, and where many hope to see their return.

From my accommodation at Moinho do Maneio, I hike through stands of oak and strawberry trees. A roe deer barks in alarm. Lush ferns reach past my waist and dozens of yellow butterflies lift and flutter as I walk. An abandoned mill appears through the trees. I feel as if I have somehow stepped out of the present, out of Portugal, even out of Europe, and into an enchanted, parallel world.

It is very still. Only the sound of the stream and the birds.

I stop at a farm on the edge of the reserve. Huge dogs with spiked collars wait by the house. Their job is to protect livestock from the wolves that have crept back into this landscape as people have left.

Albano Alavedra, the owner of the farm, offers me a beer. We sit on the terrace under an ancient oak and talk about wolves.

“Wolves make good shepherds,” he says. And good shepherds pay attention to the land, which helps both his animals and the landscape. Where there are wolves, there is no excess of anything, he says. “It is the human who throws it out of balance.”

I ask Mr. Alavedra, who grew up here, why he stayed when so many left. “My mother wanted me to get a degree,” he smiles. But his passion, he says, has always been for farming and for nature. “Only those who really liked it, stayed,” he says. “We are the only ones here now.”

Farther north, the trail crosses a medieval bridge, once the border with Spain. I stop in the evening light as martins and swallows swoop in the gloaming.

In the village of Vilar Maior, Bárbara Cardoso, an engineer and beekeeper, is visiting her elderly mother, Maria Cândida, who runs a bed-and-breakfast in their old family home. Ms. Cardoso welcomes me in and, in the morning, shows me her bees. “I like their determination,” she says. It feels like a metaphor for the whole landscape.

Dinner at the bed-and-breakfast is three courses of local cheese and honey, chickpea stew, ripe tomatoes in salt and olive oil, local wine, then dessert and several glasses of Maria Cândida’s homemade liqueur. I’m chided for not having thirds. We lack a common language, so I can only mime that I’m about to burst. She mimes back that I should eat more, then run uphill to the castle — built to defend the region against Spain. I take her advice, heading up the cobblestone streets. Each stone of the fortress is carved with the symbol of the man who made it, which is apparently how your pay was calculated if you were a stonemason in 13th-century Portugal.

Rewilding Portugal, a nonprofit conservation organization, manages tracts of land in the valley as part of an ambitious plan to accelerate the rewilding already underway. This includes reintroducing species like Sorraia horses, a local breed, and tauros, a specially bred bovine — a modern attempt to recreate the ancient and extinct aurochs, which once roamed across Europe.

Near Vilar Maior, I look for Sorraia horses. Merlin, the bird app on my phone, identifies the songs of 38 different species.

I sit on a granite boulder for breakfast. Sheep cheese on crunchy bread. The sun just cresting the ridge behind me and pushing the morning chill from the air in one hot breath. It is very still, just as it has been for days. There are signs of people everywhere — roads, stone barns, crumbling walls. But I see no one.

I catch movement in the tall grass. Something big. Not a horse. More like a dog. It is an odd feeling to want something to be a wolf while also feeling a chill of unease.

They tell stories about wolves here. That wolves steal the children, leaving only their shoes. They tell old stories, and new ones too. That environmentalists are sneaking wolves into the towns and releasing them at night. None is true.

I look again, and a family of boar snuffle out of the brush, in search of their own breakfast. There goes my wolf story.

When I find horses, it is unexpected. They trot down the path, eyeing me uncertainly, then prance away among the wildflowers, sleek and gray. A booted eagle looks sharply down from her nest as storks and buzzards soar overhead.

Farther north, I arrive at a bend in the river as evening falls and swim in the cool water. Afterward, a pair of otters appear, silky and dark in the fading light. Uphill, in the garden of Côa Honeycomb, my hotel, a cat twists around my feet. Not quite a lynx.

Fernando Romão, who runs Wildlife Portugal, a nature guiding company, takes me to look for tauros in the morning. Originally from Lisbon, Mr. Romão moved here and became obsessed with the region’s biodiversity. He is a gold mine of information about everything from rare plants to insects and wildlife, including a water snake — as richly patterned as a Persian carpet — that he points out in a stream.

We pass an ancient “wolf trap,” evidence of the region’s long and complex history with predators. (A sacrificial lamb would be left inside the stone enclosure as bait to trap.) We cut across granite boulders, brambles scratching at our legs and arms, the Côa far below.

I ask about tourism. There isn’t much, he says. People come to see birds and wildlife. Some have a hard time sleeping because they’re unaccustomed to so much silence, he says.

We round a bend and come suddenly upon a herd of tauros. They’re enormous, some weighing more than 2,000 pounds, wild and intimidating with their long horns. Together with Sorraia horses, tauros are transforming the landscape, eating and stamping and allowing oak forests — cleared for agriculture — to return. Conservationists hope that ibex and lynx will soon join them.

Later, Conceição Matos and her husband show me their farm, with accommodation downstairs and her stately family home above. Every room tells a story. One room, she tells me, was hand-painted by a French soldier who stayed during the Napoleonic wars. We descend stone steps into fields where last summer’s fires burned right up to the walls. I’m invited to dinner on the terrace. Bread and olive oil infused with thyme and rosemary from the fields, and “garden sardines” — vegetables battered and cooked as fish would be on the coast. Crisp white wine and water with a hint of fresh vervain.

Even more than the fires, Ms. Matos tells me their challenge is finding people to work. “I still believe a lot of people will come back,” she says, looking out over the cherry trees and the fields that her family has farmed for generations.

At last, the Côa nears the Douro River, where the trail ends beside the Côa Museum, overlooking the vineyards. As I get closer, my hopes of seeing a lynx or a wolf fade, but I still look and listen for howls under the waning moon.

Just south, the trail climbs to avoid a UNESCO World Heritage area that protects prehistoric rock art along the riverbank, accessible only with a guide. As the sun sets, I meet Marco Ferraz, who has run cultural and nature tours here for years and who tells me the best time to visit is at dusk.

As we approach the river, he tells me how this region was once set to be flooded for a dam, and that the discovery of prehistoric engravings became a national election issue. António Guterres, now the United Nations Secretary General, lobbied to save them while running for prime minister, and won.

We walk along the riverbank in darkness. The Côa is unseen but roaring, fed by the many tributaries I’ve crossed since that humble spring in the hills.

When the engravings appear in the flashlight, I sit in awe. Drawings of the deep past, but also now — as wildlife returns to the valley — of the present.

item.title: British Leader Arrives in Ukraine as Russia Amps Up Warnings
item.description:
Prime Minister Andy Burnham of Britain arrived in Kyiv, the Ukrainian capital, on Monday, taking a brief break from his focus on economic issues at home to make his first foreign trip since taking office.

Mr. Burnham’s visit comes as Russia has sharpened verbal attacks against Britain’s longstanding assistance to Ukraine, warning of consequences if the aid and support continue.

Mr. Burnham appeared to shrug off those warnings on Monday as British officials announced that he would present President Volodymyr Zelensky of Ukraine with technical plans for a long-range missile.

The missile, jointly built with France, is known as the Storm Shadow in Britain. Officials said that allowing the classified plans to be provided to Kyiv would allow Ukraine and France to build the French version, known as SCALP, on assembly lines inside Ukraine.

Mr. Burnham arrived in Kyiv by train on Monday morning after traveling overnight.

In a statement released by his office, Mr. Burnham said: “The friendship between our two countries will long outlast Russia’s illegal war. In both the fight and in the rebuilding to come, we will stand with Ukraine and deliver opportunities for people across both our countries.”

He added: “Russia should be in no doubt of our resolve. We will not back down until there is a just and lasting peace.”

Mr. Burnham is expected to meet with Mr. Zelensky and will be chairman of a meeting of the “coalition of the willing,” a group of leaders who have pledged support for Ukraine in the war against Russia.

Katarina Mathernova, the European Union’s ambassador to Ukraine, told reporters on Sunday night as she traveled for the coalition meeting that the mood in Ukraine had “darkened” this summer amid targeted Russian attacks on civilians.

She also noted that the war seemed to be moving into a new phase in which both sides try to inflict serious economic damage on the other. Russia is choking off Ukraine’s grain exports through the Black Sea, and Ukraine is targeting economic actors, like Wildberries, a company that is Russia’s equivalent to Amazon.

Jeanna Smialek contributed reporting from Kyiv, Ukraine.

item.title: Australia Bans Generative A.I. From Official Music Charts
item.description:
Songs that are wholly or largely created by generative A.I. will be banned from Australia’s music charts under new rules announced on Tuesday, but recordings that use the technology in a supporting role will still be allowed.

The Australian Recording Industry Association (ARIA), which oversees the charts of the country’s most popular music, said the changes will apply from Friday.

The move follows a global push by the music industry and authorities to create clearer regulation around A.I. use in music and ensure appropriate copyright protections for original artists.

ARIA’s chief executive officer, Annabelle Herd, said the music charts should reflect what Australians are listening to, but a chart that rewarded A.I. output would “undercut the very basis of the recorded music we exist to represent.”

Many artists use A.I. tools, and music charts should “keep room for that,” Ms. Herd said in a statement released by ARIA. “But music generated wholesale by services built on artists’ recordings is a different matter.”

Under the changes, recordings developed using generative A.I. will only be allowed if they are “substantially human-made” and do not raise “stream or chart manipulation concerns,” the statement said.

For example, if a song’s lead vocal or key instrumental performance is generated by A.I., the track would be ineligible, ARIA said. But a human lead vocal with A.I. backing vocals would be allowed.

Under the rules, ARIA may remove a recording from the charts if it is deemed ineligible, although artists will be allowed to appeal the decision. A.I.-generated recordings will also not qualify for the ARIA Awards — the country’s top music industry prize.

The Australian musician Ben Lee, who is known for hits like “Cigarettes Will Kill You” and “Catch My Disease,” said non-generative A.I. was used by artists in the process of music production, including for pitch correction and noise reduction. But generative A.I. and its impacts on the industry needed to be looked at more closely, he said.

“I’m not the kind of person who is at all fundamentally opposed to technological changes in my industry,” he said. “It feels like healthy pushback is a really vital part of us looking responsibly at the way to integrate these technologies into our industries.”

“I don’t see this as the endpoint. I see this as the start of a conversation,” Mr. Lee said of the chart changes.

Alexis Weaver, a composer and lecturer at the Sydney Conservatorium of Music, said ARIA’s move was a “wonderful step forward” in valuing human creativity.

The discussion about the use of A.I. in music is “exceptionally fraught and very emotional for a lot of musicians and so everyone will have a different opinion,” she told the Australian Broadcasting Corporation.

The changes come just months after a chart-topping cover of Madonna’s “Like a Prayer” angered some in the music industry who believed it was produced with A.I., the network reported this year.

The song, which has been streamed more than 48 million times on Spotify, was later updated on the music platform to include A.I. credits, the Australian Broadcasting Corporation reported.

Oliver Bown, a University of New South Wales professor studying the impacts of A.I. on the creative industries, said ARIA was the latest in a long line of organizations to develop policies banning some level of A.I.

“Everyone’s watching everyone else,” he said, pointing to governments, record labels and various music bodies across the world.

For example, the International Federation of the Phonographic Industry, which represents the recording industry worldwide, released a set of principles around generative A.I. use and chart eligibility in June. Songs that were wholly generated by A.I. were banned from charts that the federation oversees in Latin America, the Middle East, Africa and Southeast Asia. ARIA’s changes are based on the foundation’s principles.

British actors, musicians and writers welcomed the government’s decision this year to abandon its plans to let A.I. firms use copyright-protected work without permission. In the United States, a string of court cases has emerged over the misuse of A.I. and copyright.

Mr. Bown said the speed at which generative A.I. models had developed and been adopted was “unprecedented” and had sent shock waves across the broader creative industries.

But he is hopeful that the technology could also be used to create something new: “Once we establish some boundaries between ethical and unethical practices, there’s a great deal of room for people to use A.I., and to do really interesting things with it,” he said.

item.title: Chinese Artist Sentenced to Three Years in Prison for Mao Sculptures
item.description:
A Chinese court on Tuesday sentenced a prominent New York-based artist, Gao Zhen, to three years in prison for making irreverent sculptures of Mao Zedong more than 15 years ago, according to his wife.

The Sanhe City People’s Court in Hebei Province found Mr. Gao guilty of slandering one of the country’s heroes, highlighting the shrinking space for expression under China’s leader, Xi Jinping.

The case of Mr. Gao, who had emigrated to the United States and was detained in Beijing two years ago while visiting family, underlined the opacity of China’s legal system. The 70-year-old artist was tried during a one-day secret hearing in March that his family and U.S. diplomats were barred from attending. He was found guilty and sentenced during Tuesday’s hearing, which two of Mr. Gao’s other brothers were able to attend.

Mr. Gao is the elder of the artistic duo known as the Gao Brothers, who became famous during the early 2000s for their satirical and provocative takes on politically sensitive topics such as the Cultural Revolution, a decade of political turmoil unleashed by Mao, as well as the 1989 Tiananmen Square massacre.

The three-year sentence, the maximum Mr. Gao could have received, means that he will serve one more year in prison after two years’ detention. The artist plans to appeal the court’s decision.

Gao Qiang, Mr. Gao’s younger brother, who lives in New York and who worked with him on the Mao sculptures, said in a Facebook post before the sentencing that whatever the court decides, “history will ultimately judge the larger question: Whether an artist can be imprisoned for confronting history through art.”

“Gao Zhen has already lost nearly two years of freedom. He should go home,” Gao Qiang added.

Gao Zhen was arrested at his art studio on the outskirts of Beijing while visiting China in 2024. When his wife, Zhao Yaliang, tried to take the couple’s 7-year-old son, a U.S. citizen, back to the United States, she was barred from leaving. The two have remained in China, waiting for Mr. Gao’s release. Mr. Gao has refused to confess or plead guilty, according to Ms. Zhao.

The Gao brothers rose to prominence at a time of relative openness in China. While the police shut down their exhibitions, the two were able to continue working and became known for their creative antics while evading the authorities. They held underground art exhibitions and in the case of one especially provocative sculpture — a bronze statue of Mao kneeling in repentance, called “Mao’s Guilt” — they kept the head of the sculpture separate, bringing it out only for special viewings.

According to Ms. Zhao, that piece is one of three that prosecutors named in their evidence against Mr. Gao. The other two included a sculpture of Mao with breasts and a Pinocchio nose, and another that depicts a group of Mao likenesses with guns, preparing to execute Jesus.

Criticism of Mao, the former Chinese leader whose legacy is considered central to the legitimacy of the Chinese Communist Party, is strictly controlled. As part of a campaign to enforce the Party’s version of history, China has made it illegal to tarnish the reputation of historical figures or to question official narratives.

Mr. Gao was charged under that slander law, which was passed in 2018, years after he produced the sculptures of Mao. Journalists, stand-up comedians and regular citizens have been punished under the same law, but Mr. Gao’s case is one of the first times that it has been used retroactively.

People familiar with the case said Mr. Gao had been accused of disseminating images of the Mao sculptures online as recently as 2024, including on the cover of a biography of the former leader by a Chinese journalist who emigrated to the United States in the 1980s.

Shane Yi, a researcher at the nonprofit Chinese Human Rights Defenders, said that by targeting Mr. Gao, the Chinese authorities were able to remind overseas Chinese citizens that the state still had power over them whether they are abroad or back in China.

“But no matter which motive carries the most weight: A person has been locked up for two years over his art, and his wife and young son, a U.S. citizen, have been barred from leaving China this entire time,” he said.

Ms. Zhao said that her husband had been punished while in prison, including being deprived of food, and being barred from reading books and getting letters from his family.

Still, Mr. Gao has continued to make art, tearing pieces of plain paper to make portraits of his family. In a recent letter to his wife, Mr. Gao enclosed a poem: “Sleepless nights, tossing and turning, memories drift like clouds and smoke/Once a dragon slayer, now imprisoned, he has no regrets for mocking the wicked.”

Pei-Lin Wu contributed reporting.

item.title: Mass Mortality and Infected Mammals: Australia’s Bird Flu Fears Come True
item.description:
Bird flu is sweeping across Australia, devastating its unique birds and mammals, many of which are found nowhere else in the world.

Already, mass mortality events have killed more than 1,000 birds, and the disease has crossed into seals. Experts fear more deaths are likely.

Australia confirmed its first case of H5N1 in June in a migratory brown skua, a sub-Antarctic species on the country’s southern coast. Since then, the disease has rapidly spread.

To date, there have been 309 confirmed bird flu events, official data shows (the country is not counting individual bird cases, instead referring to events that could include one or more birds). Among the bird species to have died are greater crested terns, sea gulls and little penguins.

The state of South Australia has been the worst-hit, recording 194 events. More than 1,000 crested terns — a large coastal bird with a yellow bill — are believed to have died from the disease on three remote islands, the state’s leader said last week.

On Monday, the environment minister, Murray Watt, told the national broadcaster: “We are likely to see mass mortalities of birds and mammals. And I know that is a very distressing thing for Australians to hear, but we also need to be realistic.”

So far, the disease has not been detected in poultry or on farms, according to the government, and the risk to humans remains low. People who come across affected animals have been told not to touch them, but to photograph and report the sighting via official hotlines.

Euan Ritchie, a professor of wildlife ecology at Deakin University, said that while the disease had not been in Australia long, the speed of its spread was concerning.

“We have a feeling of dread that we’re only about to see the beginning of it now and it’s about to get far worse,” he said.

He added that Australia’s wildlife had evolved in isolation for millions of years, creating animals found nowhere else, such as the Australian sea lion, which is considered vulnerable, with fewer than 10,000 adults in the wild.

But this isolation also meant that the animals were more at risk of contracting new pathogens because they had not developed any immunity. This particular strain of bird flu has decimated animal populations worldwide since 2020. While Australia has had other strains of bird flu before, it successfully eradicated them. The arrival of H5N1 this year marks the first time Australia has experienced the disease, which is putting the country’s response to the test.

The Australian government began vaccinating at-risk bird species this month. Among those receiving the vaccination will be 5,000 little penguins in the state of Victoria. They are easy to vaccinate because they waddle from the ocean to their burrows each evening.

Millions in funding have also been allocated to combat the disease, including increased surveillance to ensure early detection and response.

But some conservationists and experts have criticized the government for being too slow to roll out vaccines and have called for increased investment in habitat protections.

Ariful Islam, a bird flu and epidemiology expert from Charles Sturt University, said vaccinations were not a “silver bullet,” particularly when it came to wild birds, which needed monitoring to ensure that the vaccine produced the necessary antibodies for protection from the disease.

The public is also joining the fight.

Volunteers are helping document bird deaths, particularly in South Australia. Among them is Maureen Christie, secretary of Friends of Shorebirds SE, who spends each morning searching for sick or dead birds along a patch of coastline in the town of Carpenter Rocks, and reporting them.

But the work has taken its toll.

“You can’t do anything to really help the birds,” she said.

On Monday morning, she was “elated” to find only 11 sick or dead birds. A few weeks ago, at one location, there were carcasses every few footsteps.

Yes. H5N1 has infected a range of mammals, including cows, cats, foxes and raccoons around the world. But marine mammals have been particularly hard hit. The disease killed at least 24,000 South American sea lions along the continent’s coasts in less than a year in 2023.

In Australia, authorities confirmed the first case of H5N1 in a long-nosed fur seal in South Australia last week. A second seal was suspected to have died from the disease on Monday.

Seal expert Jane Younger, from the University of Tasmania, said the disease could become an “extinction event” if it were to spread among marine mammals such as the Australian sea lion. Most of the sea lions share the same habitat in South Australia as the infected birds.

A vaccine has not yet been approved for use in Australian mammals.

“Unfortunately, there’s not really anything that can be done to stop the virus from spreading,” Ms. Younger said, adding, “it’s spread by wild animals, and we just don’t have any control over that.”
